s.u1.title: What a tissue is
s.u1.blurb: A group of cells doing one job together, and why plants organise it differently from animals.
s.u2.title: The tissue that is still dividing
s.u2.blurb: Plants grow only in certain places, and this is what is there.
s.u3.title: Tissues that have stopped dividing
s.u3.blurb: Once a cell commits to a job it cannot go back. Three kinds of simple tissue come out of that.
s.u4.title: Xylem and phloem
s.u4.blurb: The two pipes. One carries water up and is mostly dead, the other carries food and is alive.
s.u5.title: Covering and connecting
s.u5.blurb: The animal tissues that line things and the ones that hold things together.
s.u6.title: Moving and signalling
s.u6.blurb: Muscle and nerve, the two tissues that make an animal an animal.
ch6.u1.definition: A single-celled organism like Amoeba does everything with one cell: moving, eating, excreting. A body with millions of cells can afford to specialise, and it does. A tissue is a group of cells similar in structure that work together at one job. Blood, phloem and muscle are all tissues.
a.ch6-u1-read-1.title: Division of labour, inside a body
ch6.u1.sort.i0.label: A lot of supporting tissue, much of it dead
ch6.u1.sort.i0.why: Standing upright all day needs structure, and dead cells with thick walls do it cheaply.
ch6.u1.sort.i1.label: Growth limited to certain regions
ch6.u1.sort.i1.why: Which is why a plant has meristems and an animal does not.
ch6.u1.sort.i2.label: Most tissues are living
ch6.u1.sort.i2.why: Movement costs energy and dead cells cannot provide it.
ch6.u1.sort.i3.label: Growth is fairly uniform across the body
ch6.u1.sort.i3.why: No dividing regions set aside, so no meristem.
ch6.u1.sort.i4.label: More energy spent, because the body moves about
ch6.u1.sort.i4.why: Food, mates and shelter all have to be gone to.
ch6.u1.sort.i5.label: Organs and organ systems are more specialised
ch6.u1.sort.i5.why: A consequence of moving and of how they feed.
ask.ch6-u1-sort-2.deadcells.q: How can a tissue be useful if its cells are dead?
ask.ch6-u1-sort-2.deadcells.a:
Because what the plant needs from them is their walls, not their lives.

A sclerenchyma cell lays down a thick lignified wall and then dies, leaving the wall behind as a rigid tube. The husk of a coconut is this. Wood is mostly this. The cell has, in effect, spent its life manufacturing a piece of structural material and then got out of the way.

An animal cannot work like that because its supporting tissue has to grow, repair and respond, and only living cells do those.
a.ch6-u1-sort-2.title: Plant or animal, and why
a.ch6-u1-sort-2.blurb: The differences are not arbitrary. Each one follows from a plant standing still and an animal not.
ch6.u1.quiz.q0.prompt: What makes a group of cells a tissue?
ch6.u1.quiz.q0.o0: They are next to each other
ch6.u1.quiz.q0.f0: Being adjacent is not enough. Cells of different tissues sit next to each other everywhere.
ch6.u1.quiz.q0.o1: They are similar in structure and work together at one function
ch6.u1.quiz.q0.o2: They are all the same size
ch6.u1.quiz.q0.f2: Size has nothing to do with it.
ch6.u1.quiz.q0.o3: They all came from the same parent cell
ch6.u1.quiz.q0.f3: True of many tissues, but it is not what defines one.
ch6.u1.quiz.q1.prompt: Why do plants have more dead supporting tissue than animals?
ch6.u1.quiz.q1.o1: Plants need to stand upright, and dead thick-walled cells do that cheaply
ch6.u1.quiz.q1.f1: Right. The wall is what does the supporting, and it works after the cell has gone.
ch6.u1.quiz.q1.f2: They do not. Many plant cells outlive any animal.
ch6.u1.quiz.q1.f3: True of vertebrates, but it is not why plant tissue is dead.
a.ch6-u1-quiz-3.title: What a tissue is
ch6.u2.onion.predict.prompt: You cut 1 cm off the root tips of one onion on day 4. What happens to those roots afterwards?
ch6.u2.onion.predict.o0: They grow back faster than before
ch6.u2.onion.predict.o1: They go on growing at the same rate
ch6.u2.onion.predict.o2: They stop growing, or nearly so
ch6.u2.onion.observe: Compare the two jars on day 5. Which one gained length?
ch6.u2.onion.explain: The dividing tissue sits at the very tip. Cut the tip off and you have removed the only part that was making new cells, so that root stops lengthening while the untrimmed one carries on.
ch6.u2.do.steps:
1. Fill both jars with water and sit an onion on each so the base just touches.
2. Leave them somewhere light and let roots grow for a few days.
3. Measure the roots on day 1, day 2 and day 3 and write the lengths in a table.
4. On day 4, cut about 1 cm off the root tips of the onion in jar 2 only.
5. Keep measuring both for five more days.
ch6.u2.do.watch: Measure from the same point each day or the numbers will wander. The result is a comparison between two jars, so a careless measurement in one of them is what will mislead you, not a slow day's growth.
a.ch6-u2-do-1.title: Cut the root tips and watch
a.ch6-u2-do-1.blurb: Two onions growing roots in water. Trim one and compare, over five days.
ch6.u2.definition: Meristematic tissue is the dividing tissue, and it sits only where a plant actually grows. Apical meristem is at the tips of stems and roots and makes them longer. Lateral meristem, the cambium, sits in a ring and makes the stem thicker. Intercalary meristem sits near the node, which is how grass regrows after it is cut. Its cells are small, densely packed, thin-walled and have no vacuole.
a.ch6-u2-read-2.title: Three places a plant grows
ch6.u2.sort.i0.label: Makes a root longer
ch6.u2.sort.i0.why: At the very tip, which is why cutting the tip stops it.
ch6.u2.sort.i1.label: Makes a stem taller
ch6.u2.sort.i1.why: Same tissue, other end of the plant.
ch6.u2.sort.i2.label: Makes a trunk thicker
ch6.u2.sort.i2.why: Also called cambium. A ring, not a point.
ch6.u2.sort.i3.label: Adds girth to a root
ch6.u2.sort.i4.label: Lets cut grass grow back
ch6.u2.sort.i4.why: Near the node, below where the mower passed.
ch6.u2.sort.i5.label: Sits near the node
ch6.u2.sort.i5.why: Which is what puts it below the damage.
ask.ch6-u2-sort-3.grass.q: Why does a lawn survive mowing when a hedge needs careful pruning?
ask.ch6-u2-sort-3.grass.a:
Because grass keeps its growing tissue low down and a hedge keeps it at the tips.

Grass has intercalary meristem near the base of each leaf, so a mower passes above it and takes only finished tissue. The growing point is untouched and the blade simply pushes up again.

Most broad-leaved plants grow from apical meristem at the tips, so cutting the tip removes the factory. The plant responds by activating side buds instead, which is why pruning makes a hedge bushier rather than taller. It is the same tissue biology behind both.
a.ch6-u2-sort-3.title: Which meristem does this?
ch6.u2.quiz.q0.o0: In a ring around the stem
ch6.u2.quiz.q0.f0: That is lateral meristem, the cambium.
ch6.u2.quiz.q0.o1: At the tips of stems and roots
ch6.u2.quiz.q0.f1: Right, and it is why trimming a root tip stops that root lengthening.
ch6.u2.quiz.q0.f3: Plant growth is localised. That is the whole difference from an animal.
ch6.u2.quiz.q1.prompt: Meristematic cells have no vacuole. Why would that be?
ch6.u2.quiz.q1.o0: They are too small to have one
ch6.u2.quiz.q1.f0: Size is a consequence of being newly divided, not the reason.
ch6.u2.quiz.q1.o1: A big vacuole stores things, and these cells are dividing rather than storing
ch6.u2.quiz.q1.f1: Right. Dense cytoplasm and a prominent nucleus is what a cell geared to divide looks like.
ch6.u2.quiz.q1.o2: Vacuoles only exist in animal cells
ch6.u2.quiz.q1.f2: Vacuoles are a plant cell feature, and large ones especially.
ch6.u2.quiz.q1.o3: They lost them when they divided
ch6.u2.quiz.q1.f3: Division does not strip a cell of its organelles.
a.ch6-u2-quiz-4.title: The dividing tissue
ch6.u3.definition: A cell made by a meristem does not stay a meristem cell. It takes on a shape, a size and a job, and loses the ability to divide. That process is differentiation, and what it produces is permanent tissue. Simple permanent tissue is made of one kind of cell; complex permanent tissue is made of several working together.
a.ch6-u3-read-1.title: Committing to a job
ch6.u3.sort.i0.label: Thin walls, loosely packed, living
ch6.u3.sort.i0.why: The default plant cell, and the one that stores food.
ch6.u3.sort.i1.label: Has large air cavities to help a water plant float
ch6.u3.sort.i1.why: Aerenchyma, which is parenchyma with air spaces.
ch6.u3.sort.i2.label: Contains chloroplasts and photosynthesises
ch6.u3.sort.i2.why: Chlorenchyma. Still parenchyma, with chloroplasts added.
ch6.u3.sort.i3.label: Living, with walls thickened irregularly at the corners
ch6.u3.sort.i3.why: Which is what makes a stem bend instead of snapping.
ch6.u3.sort.i4.label: Gives tendrils and climbing stems their flexibility
ch6.u3.sort.i4.why: Found in leaf stalks, just under the epidermis.
ch6.u3.sort.i5.label: Dead cells with thick lignified walls
ch6.u3.sort.i5.why: No living contents at all, just the tube the wall left behind.
ch6.u3.sort.i6.label: Makes the husk of a coconut hard
ch6.u3.sort.i7.label: Long, narrow, with no space inside the cell
ch6.u3.sort.i7.why: The wall grew inwards until the lumen nearly closed.
a.ch6-u3-sort-2.title: Parenchyma, collenchyma or sclerenchyma?
a.ch6-u3-sort-2.blurb: Three simple tissues, told apart by their walls. Exercise 4 asks exactly this.
ch6.u3.do.steps:
1. Stretch the leaf and break it gently, so a thin skin peels out from the cut.
2. Remove that peel and float it in a petri dish of water.
3. Add a few drops of safranin and wait a couple of minutes.
4. Transfer the peel to a slide and lower a cover slip onto it.
5. Look for small pores, each one held between a pair of kidney-shaped cells.
ch6.u3.do.watch: A peel that tears or folds will show as a dark double layer and nothing will be clear through it. Tear slowly and take the thinnest piece you get rather than the biggest.
ask.ch6-u3-do-3.stomataopen.q: If stomata let water escape, why does the plant have them at all?
ask.ch6-u3-do-3.stomataopen.a:
Because it has no choice. The same pores that lose water are the only way carbon dioxide gets in, and without that there is no photosynthesis.

So the plant is stuck with a trade: open the stomata and lose water, close them and starve. The guard cells are how it manages the compromise minute by minute, swelling to open the pore when conditions are good and going slack to close it when water is short. A desert plant resolves the same trade differently, with a thick waxy cuticle and stomata that open at night.
a.ch6-u3-do-3.title: Peel a leaf and find the pores
a.ch6-u3-do-3.blurb: The epidermis comes off in a transparent sheet, and the stomata are visible in it.
ch6.u3.sort2.i0.label: Usually a single layer of cells
ch6.u3.sort2.i0.why: Thicker only in plants from very dry places.
ch6.u3.sort2.i1.label: Secretes a waxy cutin on the outer surface
ch6.u3.sort2.i1.why: Which is what resists water loss and fungal attack.
ch6.u3.sort2.i2.label: Carries root hairs that absorb water
ch6.u3.sort2.i2.why: Long projections that raise the absorbing surface.
ch6.u3.sort2.i3.label: Contains the stomata
ch6.u3.sort2.i4.label: Dead cells, compactly arranged with no gaps
ch6.u3.sort2.i4.why: Which is why bark is impervious.
ch6.u3.sort2.i5.label: Walls contain suberin
ch6.u3.sort2.i5.why: A substance gases and water cannot pass.
ch6.u3.sort2.i6.label: Formed by secondary meristem as the plant ages
ch6.u3.sort2.i6.why: It replaces the epidermis on an older branch.
a.ch6-u3-sort-4.title: The protective layers
ch6.u3.quiz.q0.prompt: Which tissue makes the husk of a coconut?
ch6.u3.quiz.q0.f1: Collenchyma bends. A coconut husk does not.
ch6.u3.quiz.q0.f2: Right. Dead cells with thick lignified walls.
ch6.u3.quiz.q0.f3: The epidermis is a surface layer, not the bulk of a husk.
ch6.u3.quiz.q1.prompt: What is the role of the epidermis in a plant?
ch6.u3.quiz.q1.o0: It divides to make new cells
ch6.u3.quiz.q1.f0: That is meristem. The epidermis is permanent tissue.
ch6.u3.quiz.q1.o1: It protects all the parts, and limits water loss
ch6.u3.quiz.q1.f1: Right, with help from the waxy cutin on its outer surface.
a.ch6-u3-quiz-5.title: Simple permanent tissue
ch6.u4.definition: Complex tissue is made of more than one kind of cell, all coordinating on one job. Xylem carries water and minerals upwards and is made of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres, most of them dead with thick walls. Phloem carries food and is made of sieve cells, sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibres and phloem parenchyma, and all of it is living except the fibres. Together they form a vascular bundle, which is what made life on land possible.
a.ch6-u4-read-1.title: Two pipes, built differently
ch6.u4.sort.i0.label: Tracheids
ch6.u4.sort.i1.label: Vessels
ch6.u4.sort.i1.why: The wide tubes that carry the bulk of the water.
ch6.u4.sort.i2.label: Xylem fibres
ch6.u4.sort.i3.label: Sieve tubes
ch6.u4.sort.i3.why: Tubular cells with perforated end walls.
ch6.u4.sort.i4.label: Companion cells
ch6.u4.sort.i4.why: Alive, and they keep the sieve tubes working.
ch6.u4.sort.i5.label: Phloem fibres
ch6.u4.sort.i5.why: The one part of phloem that is dead.
ch6.u4.sort.i6.label: Carries water and minerals upwards only
ch6.u4.sort.i7.label: Carries food from the leaves to the rest of the plant
ch6.u4.sort.i7.why: Which can mean downwards, upwards or sideways.
ask.ch6-u4-sort-2.whydead.q: Why is xylem mostly dead while phloem has to be alive?
ask.ch6-u4-sort-2.whydead.a:
Because of what each one is moving, and what moves it.

Water in xylem is pulled from above. Evaporation at the leaves puts the whole column under tension and drags it up, so the xylem needs to be an open pipe strong enough not to collapse. A dead cell with a thick lignified wall is the ideal pipe, and living contents would only get in the way.

Food in phloem is pushed, and the pushing is done by the cells themselves loading sugar in at one end and unloading at the other. That takes energy, so the cells have to be alive. The companion cell exists precisely to supply it.
a.ch6-u4-sort-2.title: Xylem or phloem?
a.ch6-u4-sort-2.blurb: Exercise 2 asks what xylem is made of. This is that question, both ways round.
a.ch6-u4-tree-3.title: Complete the permanent tissue chart
a.ch6-u4-tree-3.blurb: The chart the last exercise asks you to fill in. Two questions place any permanent tissue.
ch6.u4.quiz.q0.prompt: How many kinds of cell make up xylem tissue?
ch6.u4.quiz.q0.f2: Right: tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.
ch6.u4.quiz.q0.f3: One kind of cell would make it a simple tissue, not a complex one.
ch6.u4.quiz.q1.prompt: Which tissue transports food in a plant?
ch6.u4.quiz.q1.f0: Xylem carries water and minerals, and only upwards.
ch6.u4.quiz.q1.f1: Right, and in whichever direction the plant needs it.
ch6.u4.quiz.q1.f2: Parenchyma stores food rather than transporting it.
a.ch6-u4-quiz-4.title: The conducting tissues
ch6.u5.epithelial: Epithelial tissue covers and lines: the skin, the mouth, blood vessels, lung alveoli, kidney tubules. Its cells are packed tightly with almost nothing between them, so anything entering or leaving the body has to cross at least one layer of it. That is what makes it a barrier and a filter at the same time.
a.ch6-u5-read-1.title: Tissue that lines things
ch6.u5.sort.i0.label: Extremely thin and flat, lining lung alveoli
ch6.u5.sort.i0.why: Thin because gases have to cross it.
ch6.u5.sort.i1.label: Lines blood vessels
ch6.u5.sort.i1.why: Same reason: a thin barrier to cross.
ch6.u5.sort.i2.label: Many layers, in skin
ch6.u5.sort.i2.why: Layered to survive wear and tear.
ch6.u5.sort.i3.label: Tall cells lining the intestine
ch6.u5.sort.i3.why: Height gives surface area for absorption.
ch6.u5.sort.i4.label: Tall cells with cilia, in the respiratory tract
ch6.u5.sort.i4.why: Ciliated columnar. The cilia push mucus along.
ch6.u5.sort.i5.label: Cube-shaped, lining kidney tubules
ch6.u5.sort.i5.why: Where it also provides mechanical support.
ch6.u5.sort.i6.label: Found in the ducts of salivary glands
a.ch6-u5-sort-2.title: Which epithelium, and where?
a.ch6-u5-sort-2.blurb: The shape follows the job every time. Flat where things cross, tall where things are absorbed.
ch6.u5.connective: In connective tissue the cells are spaced out and sit in a matrix between them, and it is the matrix that decides what the tissue does. Fluid matrix gives blood. Hard matrix of calcium and phosphorus gives bone. A tough fibrous matrix gives tendon and ligament. A solid matrix of proteins and sugars gives cartilage.
a.ch6-u5-read-3.title: Tissue that holds things together
ch6.u5.sort2.i0.label: Fluid matrix called plasma
ch6.u5.sort2.i0.why: With red cells, white cells and platelets suspended in it.
ch6.u5.sort2.i1.label: Hard matrix of calcium and phosphorus
ch6.u5.sort2.i1.why: Which is what anchors the muscles.
ch6.u5.sort2.i2.label: Connects bone to bone, and is very elastic
ch6.u5.sort2.i3.label: Connects muscle to bone, strong but not flexible
ch6.u5.sort2.i3.why: The pairing people most often get the wrong way round.
ch6.u5.sort2.i4.label: Smooths the surface at a joint
ch6.u5.sort2.i4.why: Also in the nose, ear, trachea and larynx.
ch6.u5.sort2.i5.label: Found in the ear, which is why it folds
ch6.u5.sort2.i5.why: Fold an ear and it springs back. A bone would not.
ch6.u5.sort2.i6.label: Fills the space inside organs and repairs tissue
ch6.u5.sort2.i6.why: Between skin and muscle, around vessels and nerves.
ch6.u5.sort2.i7.label: Stores fat below the skin and insulates
ask.ch6-u5-sort-4.whyonecategory.q: Blood is a liquid and bone is rock hard. How can they possibly be the same kind of tissue?
ask.ch6-u5-sort-4.whyonecategory.a:
Because the category is about the arrangement, not the substance.

In every connective tissue the cells sit apart from one another, embedded in a matrix they secreted themselves, and the matrix does most of the work. Change the matrix and you change the tissue completely: make it fluid and you get blood, load it with calcium and phosphorus and you get bone, spin it into tough fibres and you get tendon.

So the seven are one family in the way that a rope, a net and a sheet are one family. It is the same trick, used at different settings, and noticing that is easier than holding seven unrelated facts.
a.ch6-u5-sort-4.title: Which connective tissue?
a.ch6-u5-sort-4.blurb: Seven of them. The memory aid above the section is for exactly this list.
ch6.u5.quiz.q0.prompt: Which tissue connects a muscle to a bone?
ch6.u5.quiz.q0.f0: A ligament joins bone to bone, and is the elastic one.
ch6.u5.quiz.q0.f1: Right. Strong, fibrous, and not very flexible.
ch6.u5.quiz.q0.f2: Cartilage cushions joints rather than attaching anything.
ch6.u5.quiz.q1.prompt: Why is blood called a connective tissue?
ch6.u5.quiz.q1.f0: It does not join one organ to another the way a ligament joins bones.
ch6.u5.quiz.q1.o1: Because its cells are spaced out in a matrix, which is what defines connective tissue
ch6.u5.quiz.q1.f1: Right. The matrix happens to be a fluid, plasma, but the pattern is the same.
ch6.u5.quiz.q1.o2: Because it clots and sticks things together
ch6.u5.quiz.q1.f2: Clotting is a function, not the reason for the classification.
ch6.u5.quiz.q1.o3: Because it is found everywhere in the body
ch6.u5.quiz.q1.f3: Being widespread is not what puts a tissue in a category.
a.ch6-u5-quiz-5.title: Covering and connecting
ch6.u6.muscle: Muscle cells are long, which is why they are called fibres, and they contain proteins that contract. Striated muscle is attached to bone, shows light and dark bands, has many nuclei, and you control it. Smooth muscle is spindle-shaped with one nucleus, lines the gut and the blood vessels, and you do not. Cardiac muscle is branched, striated and has one nucleus, and it has been contracting without rest since before you were born.
a.ch6-u6-read-1.title: Three kinds of muscle
ch6.u6.sort.i0.label: Attached to bones, and moves the body
ch6.u6.sort.i0.why: Also called skeletal muscle for that reason.
ch6.u6.sort.i1.label: Long, cylindrical, unbranched, many nuclei
ch6.u6.sort.i1.why: Multinucleate, which is unusual for an animal cell.
ch6.u6.sort.i2.label: You decide when it contracts
ch6.u6.sort.i3.label: Spindle-shaped with pointed ends, one nucleus
ch6.u6.sort.i3.why: No bands, which is why it is also called unstriated.
ch6.u6.sort.i4.label: Found in the iris of the eye and in the ureters
ch6.u6.sort.i5.label: Moves food along the alimentary canal
ch6.u6.sort.i5.why: Which you cannot start or stop by wanting to.
ch6.u6.sort.i6.label: Branched, striated, one nucleus
ch6.u6.sort.i6.why: The only muscle that is both striated and involuntary.
ch6.u6.sort.i7.label: Contracts rhythmically without ever resting
ch6.u6.sort.i7.why: For a lifetime, which no other muscle manages.
a.ch6-u6-sort-2.title: Striated, smooth or cardiac?
a.ch6-u6-sort-2.blurb: Exercise 8 asks you to tell these three apart. Shape, nuclei, and whether you can choose.
ch6.neuron.body.label: The cell body
ch6.neuron.body.do: Draw a rounded blob a little left of centre, about the size of a thumbnail.
ch6.neuron.body.does: The cell body holds the cytoplasm and the nucleus. Everything else on this diagram is an extension of it.
ch6.neuron.nucleus.label: The nucleus
ch6.neuron.nucleus.do: Put a small circle inside the blob, off to one side.
ch6.neuron.nucleus.does: The nucleus, as in any cell. A neuron keeps one and never divides again after it forms.
ch6.neuron.dendrites.label: The dendrites
ch6.neuron.dendrites.do: Draw five short branching lines spreading out from the left side of the blob.
ch6.neuron.dendrites.does: Dendrites receive. A signal arriving from another neuron lands here, and there are many of them because one neuron listens to many others.
ch6.neuron.axon.label: The axon
ch6.neuron.axon.do: Draw one long line from the right side of the blob, running most of the way across the page.
ch6.neuron.axon.does: The axon carries the signal away, and only one leaves each neuron. In a human it can run from the base of the spine to the toe, which makes a single cell a metre long.
ch6.neuron.axon.detail.p0: A neuron has many dendrites and exactly one axon.
ch6.neuron.axon.detail.p1: The signal travelling along it is a nerve impulse.
ch6.neuron.axon.detail.p2: Many axons bundled together by connective tissue make a nerve.
ch6.neuron.axon.detail.p3: An individual nerve cell may be up to a metre long.
ch6.neuron.endings.label: The nerve endings
ch6.neuron.endings.do: Split the far end of the long line into three short branches.
ch6.neuron.endings.does: The endings pass the signal on, to another neuron or to a muscle. Nerve meeting muscle is what turns a decision into a movement.
ch6.neuron.caption: A neuron, the unit of nervous tissue
ask.ch6-u6-draw-3.direction.q: Does a signal ever travel the other way along a neuron?
ask.ch6-u6-draw-3.direction.a:
No, and the shape of the cell is why.

Dendrites receive and the axon transmits, and the junction at the far end only passes a signal one way: the ending releases a chemical, and the next cell has receptors for it. The receiving cell has nothing to release back and the sending cell has nothing to receive with.

That one-way valve at every junction is what lets a nervous system carry information in a definite direction rather than just buzzing. It is also why a signal from your foot reaches your brain and not the other way round along the same fibre.
a.ch6-u6-draw-3.title: Draw a neuron, part by part
a.ch6-u6-draw-3.blurb: Five steps, in the order a signal travels. Exercise 9 asks for this diagram labelled.
ch6.u6.quiz.q0.prompt: Which muscle is both striated and involuntary?
ch6.u6.quiz.q0.f0: Skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary.
ch6.u6.quiz.q0.f1: Smooth muscle is involuntary but has no striations.
ch6.u6.quiz.q0.f2: Right. Cardiac muscle is the one that is both, and it is branched as well.
ch6.u6.quiz.q0.f3: Cardiac muscle is exactly this combination.
ch6.u6.quiz.q1.prompt: How many axons does a neuron have?
ch6.u6.quiz.q1.f0: Dendrites are many. The axon is not.
ch6.u6.quiz.q1.f1: Right. Many dendrites in, one axon out.
ch6.u6.quiz.q1.f2: Without an axon the cell could not pass a signal on at all.
ch6.u6.quiz.q1.o3: One for each muscle it reaches
ch6.u6.quiz.q1.f3: One axon can branch at its end to reach several targets, but it is still one axon.
a.ch6-u6-quiz-4.title: Muscle and nerve
mis.adjacent-makes-tissue.statement: Cells that sit next to each other form a tissue.
mis.adjacent-makes-tissue.correction: They must also be similar and share a function. Neighbouring cells often belong to different tissues.
mis.size-makes-tissue.statement: A tissue is cells of the same size.
mis.size-makes-tissue.correction: Structure and shared function define it, not size.
mis.origin-makes-tissue.statement: A tissue is any group of cells from one parent cell.
mis.origin-makes-tissue.correction: Common origin is usual but it is not the definition. The shared job is.
mis.plants-cannot-repair.statement: Plants cannot repair damaged cells, so their tissue dies.
mis.plants-cannot-repair.correction: Plants repair and regrow readily. Dead supporting tissue is a design that works, not a failure.
mis.plant-cells-die-fast.statement: Plant cells die sooner than animal cells.
mis.plant-cells-die-fast.correction: Many live for decades. Sclerenchyma dies because its job needs only the wall.
mis.bones-explain-it.statement: Plants need dead tissue because they have no bones.
mis.bones-explain-it.correction: Most animals have no bones either. The real reason is standing still and standing upright.
mis.apical-is-lateral.statement: Apical meristem runs in a ring around the stem.
mis.apical-is-lateral.correction: That is lateral meristem, the cambium. Apical sits at the tips.
mis.apical-is-intercalary.statement: Apical meristem sits near the nodes.
mis.apical-is-intercalary.correction: That is intercalary meristem. Apical is at the very tip.
mis.growth-is-everywhere.statement: A plant grows evenly all over, like an animal.
mis.growth-is-everywhere.correction: Plant growth is confined to meristems. That is one of the main differences from an animal.
mis.too-small-for-vacuole.statement: Meristematic cells have no vacuole because they are too small.
mis.too-small-for-vacuole.correction: A cell geared to dividing carries dense cytoplasm and a large nucleus instead. The size follows from that.
mis.vacuole-is-animal.statement: Vacuoles are an animal cell feature.
mis.vacuole-is-animal.correction: Large vacuoles are characteristic of plant cells.
mis.division-removes-vacuole.statement: Dividing strips a cell of its vacuole.
mis.division-removes-vacuole.correction: Division does not remove organelles. These cells never built a large one.
mis.parenchyma-is-hard.statement: Parenchyma is what makes plant parts hard.
mis.parenchyma-is-hard.correction: Parenchyma is thin-walled and soft. Sclerenchyma is the hard one.
mis.collenchyma-is-hard.correction: Collenchyma bends. It gives flexibility, not rigidity.
mis.epidermis-is-bulk.statement: The epidermis makes up the bulk of a husk or stem.
mis.epidermis-is-bulk.correction: It is a surface layer, usually one cell thick.
mis.epidermis-divides.statement: The epidermis is a dividing tissue.
mis.epidermis-divides.correction: It is permanent tissue. Meristem is what divides.
mis.epidermis-transports.statement: The epidermis transports water through the plant.
mis.epidermis-transports.correction: Xylem does that. The epidermis covers and protects.
mis.epidermis-stores.statement: The epidermis is where a plant stores food.
mis.epidermis-stores.correction: Parenchyma stores food. The epidermis is a covering.
mis.xylem-has-two.statement: Xylem is made of two kinds of cell.
mis.xylem-has-two.correction: Four: tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.
mis.xylem-has-three.statement: Xylem is made of three kinds of cell.
mis.xylem-has-three.correction: Four. The fibres are easy to forget.
mis.xylem-is-simple.correction: A simple tissue is one kind of cell. Xylem has four, which makes it complex.
mis.xylem-carries-food.statement: Xylem carries food around the plant.
mis.xylem-carries-food.correction: Xylem carries water and minerals, upwards only. Phloem carries food.
mis.parenchyma-transports.statement: Parenchyma is the plant's transport tissue.
mis.parenchyma-transports.correction: It stores. Transport is xylem and phloem.
mis.ligament-joins-muscle.statement: A ligament joins muscle to bone.
mis.ligament-joins-muscle.correction: A tendon does that. A ligament joins bone to bone.
mis.cartilage-attaches.correction: Cartilage cushions and smooths joints. Tendons attach.
mis.areolar-attaches.statement: Areolar tissue attaches muscle to bone.
mis.areolar-attaches.correction: Areolar tissue fills space and repairs.
mis.blood-connects-organs.statement: Blood is connective tissue because it physically joins organs.
mis.blood-connects-organs.correction: It is connective because its cells sit spaced out in a matrix, which here happens to be fluid.
mis.clotting-defines-it.statement: Blood is connective tissue because it clots.
mis.clotting-defines-it.correction: Clotting is something it does. The matrix is why it is classified where it is.
mis.widespread-defines-it.statement: Blood is connective tissue because it is everywhere.
mis.widespread-defines-it.correction: Being widespread is not a category. The matrix is.
mis.skeletal-is-involuntary.correction: You decide when to move a limb. It is the voluntary one.
mis.smooth-is-striated.correction: It does not, which is why it is also called unstriated.
mis.no-striated-involuntary.statement: No muscle is both striated and involuntary.
mis.no-striated-involuntary.correction: Cardiac muscle is both, and branched as well.
mis.many-axons.correction: It has exactly one. The many branches are the dendrites.
mis.no-axon.correction: Without one it could not pass a signal on.
mis.axon-per-target.statement: A neuron grows one axon for each place it reaches.
mis.axon-per-target.correction: One axon leaves the cell. It may branch at the far end, which is a different thing.
recap.s.u1.q1.answer: A group of cells similar in structure that work together to carry out one function. Blood, phloem and muscle are all tissues.
recap.s.u1.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'a group of cells' and nothing more. Any lump of a body is a group of cells; the shared structure and the shared job are what matter.
recap.s.u1.q2.ask: Why do plants contain so much dead tissue and animals so little?
recap.s.u1.q2.answer: A plant stands still and has to hold itself upright, and a thick dead cell wall does that cheaply. An animal moves, which takes energy, so its tissues have to be alive.
recap.s.u1.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'because plants are not alive in the same way'. Plants are entirely alive; it is specific tissues that trade their contents for a useful wall.
recap.s.u2.q1.ask: You cut the tips off a plant's roots. What happens to those roots, and why?
recap.s.u2.q1.answer: They stop lengthening. The apical meristem, the only dividing tissue in a root, sits right at the tip and has been removed.
recap.s.u2.q1.listenFor: Listen for 'they grow back faster'. Damage prompting regrowth is a reasonable guess and the opposite of what happens, because the growing tissue itself is what was cut off.
recap.s.u2.q2.ask: Grass survives being mown every week. Why does that not kill it?
recap.s.u2.q2.answer: Its intercalary meristem sits near the base of the leaf, below the height of the blade, so the growing tissue is never removed.
recap.s.u2.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'grass grows fast'. Speed is not the point; the position of the meristem is.
recap.s.u3.q1.ask: Parenchyma, collenchyma and sclerenchyma. Tell them apart by their walls.
recap.s.u3.q1.answer: Parenchyma has thin walls and is living. Collenchyma is living with walls thickened irregularly at the corners, which lets a stem bend. Sclerenchyma is dead with thick lignified walls, which makes a part hard.
recap.s.u3.q1.listenFor: Listen for sclerenchyma described as living. The cells die, and the tissue works afterwards because the wall is the useful part.
recap.s.u3.q2.ask: What are stomata for, and what do they cost the plant?
recap.s.u3.q2.answer: They let carbon dioxide in for photosynthesis, and let water vapour out as transpiration. The plant cannot have one without the other, so guard cells open and close them.
recap.s.u3.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'to let the plant breathe' with nothing about water. The cost is the interesting half, and it is what shapes desert plants.
recap.s.u4.q1.ask: Name the four kinds of cell in xylem.
recap.s.u4.q1.answer: Tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres.
recap.s.u4.q1.listenFor: Listen for two or three. The fibres and the parenchyma are the ones that get dropped, because they are supportive and storage rather than conducting.
recap.s.u4.q2.ask: Xylem is mostly dead and phloem is mostly alive. Why the difference?
recap.s.u4.q2.answer: Water in xylem is pulled up by evaporation at the leaves, so it needs an open rigid pipe and nothing else. Food in phloem is pushed by the cells themselves loading and unloading sugar, which takes energy and therefore living cells.
recap.s.u4.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'because water does not need living cells'. True but incomplete: the real contrast is that one is pulled from outside and the other is pushed from within.
recap.s.u5.q1.ask: Lung alveoli are lined with extremely thin flat cells. Why that shape?
recap.s.u5.q1.answer: Because gases have to cross the lining. A thin flat squamous cell is the shortest path from the air to the blood.
recap.s.u5.q1.listenFor: Listen for an answer about the cells being weak or undeveloped. Thinness here is the specialisation, not a shortfall.
recap.s.u5.q2.ask: Which joins bone to bone, and which joins muscle to bone?
recap.s.u5.q2.answer: Ligament joins bone to bone and is very elastic. Tendon joins muscle to bone and is strong but not flexible.
recap.s.u5.q2.listenFor: Listen for them swapped. It is the single most common confusion in this chapter, and the word tendon sounding like tension does not help.
recap.s.u6.q1.ask: Cardiac muscle is unusual. What two things does it combine that no other muscle does?
recap.s.u6.q1.answer: It is striated, like skeletal muscle, and involuntary, like smooth muscle. It is also branched, and it contracts rhythmically without rest for a lifetime.
recap.s.u6.q1.listenFor: Listen for cardiac muscle called voluntary because it is striated. Striation usually goes with voluntary control, and the heart is the exception that breaks the pairing.
recap.s.u6.q2.ask: A neuron has many dendrites and one axon. What does that asymmetry tell you?
recap.s.u6.q2.answer: That the cell listens widely and speaks once. Many dendrites gather signals from many other neurons, and the single axon carries one decision away.
recap.s.u6.q2.listenFor: Listen for 'it has many axons'. The diagram makes the dendrites look like more of the same thing, and the difference between receiving and transmitting is the whole point.
aid.s.u5.meaning: Seven connective tissues, which is more than anyone holds as a list. The word is a reminder that all seven are the same idea: cells spaced out in a matrix, with the matrix deciding the job.
aid.s.u5.P.property: Plasma, the fluid matrix that makes blood a connective tissue
aid.s.u5.P.note: Blood carries gases, food, hormones and waste.
aid.s.u5.L.note: Very elastic, and very little matrix.
aid.s.u5.A.property: Areolar, the packing between skin and muscle
aid.s.u5.A.note: Fills space inside organs and helps repair.
aid.s.u5.S.property: Skeleton, which is to say bone
aid.s.u5.S.note: A hard matrix of calcium and phosphorus.
aid.s.u5.I.property: Insulating fat, which is adipose tissue
aid.s.u5.I.note: Cells full of fat globules, below the skin.
aid.s.u5.C.property: Cartilage, at the joints and in the ear
aid.s.u5.C.note: A solid matrix of proteins and sugars, which bends.

gloss.tissue: A group of cells similar in structure that work together to carry out one function.
gloss.meristem: The dividing tissue of a plant, found only where the plant grows: at tips, in a ring as cambium, and near the nodes.
gloss.cambium: The lateral meristem, a ring of dividing tissue that makes a stem or root thicker.
gloss.differentiation: The process by which a cell made by a meristem takes on a permanent shape, size and job, and loses the ability to divide.
gloss.permanent-tissue: Tissue whose cells have differentiated and no longer divide. Simple if it is one kind of cell, complex if several.
gloss.parenchyma: Thin-walled living cells, loosely packed, which store food. With chloroplasts it is chlorenchyma; with air cavities, aerenchyma.
gloss.collenchyma: Living cells with walls thickened irregularly at the corners, giving a stem or tendril the ability to bend without breaking.
gloss.sclerenchyma: Dead cells with thick walls hardened by lignin, which make a part rigid. The husk of a coconut is this.
gloss.lignin: The substance that hardens a plant cell wall and makes wood stiff.
gloss.stomata: Pores in the epidermis of a leaf, each held between two guard cells, through which gases are exchanged and water vapour is lost.
gloss.guard-cell: One of a pair of kidney-shaped cells that open and close a stoma.
gloss.transpiration: The loss of water as vapour from a plant, mostly through the stomata.
gloss.epidermis: The outermost layer of cells on a plant, usually one cell thick, which protects it and limits water loss.
gloss.cork: Dead, compactly arranged cells formed as a plant ages, with suberin in their walls making them impervious to gases and water.
gloss.xylem: The complex tissue that carries water and minerals upwards. Tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres, mostly dead.
gloss.phloem: The complex tissue that carries food from the leaves. Sieve cells, sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem fibres and phloem parenchyma, all living except the fibres.
gloss.epithelial: The animal tissue that covers and lines: skin, mouth, blood vessels, alveoli, kidney tubules. Its cells are tightly packed with almost no gaps.
gloss.squamous: Flat, scale-like epithelial cells, extremely thin where substances must cross, as in the alveoli. In layers, in skin, it is stratified squamous.
gloss.connective: Animal tissue in which the cells are spaced out in a matrix. The matrix decides the job: fluid gives blood, hard gives bone, fibrous gives tendon.
gloss.matrix: The material between the cells of a connective tissue. It may be fluid, jelly-like, dense or rigid.
gloss.ligament: Connective tissue joining bone to bone. Very elastic, with little matrix.
gloss.tendon: Connective tissue joining muscle to bone. Great strength, limited flexibility.
gloss.neuron: The unit of nervous tissue: a cell body with a nucleus, many short dendrites that receive, and one long axon that transmits.
gloss.axon: The single long fibre that carries a nerve impulse away from a neuron. It can be a metre long.
gloss.dendrite: One of the many short branches of a neuron that receive signals from other cells.
